defaults.permitted_development: Across Somerset, householder boundary works are normally allowed without a planning application up to 2 metres in height, dropping to 1 metre beside a highway used by vehicles or its footpath. Those usual limits do not override listed-building controls or any local condition that removes permitted development rights.

rules.height_rules: Across Somerset, the usual boundary limits are 2 metres overall, or 1 metre where the enclosure sits next to a highway used by vehicles. A site that has been raised, terraced or fronted by a retaining wall can reach those limits faster than homeowners expect.
rules.depth_rules: Across Somerset, boundary enclosures do not have a national depth rule. The more useful checks are where the line sits, whether it encroaches visually on the frontage, and whether it also acts as a retaining wall.
rules.boundary_rules: Across Somerset, boundary works that sit by a driveway, corner plot or junction still need safe visibility. The normal right is also restricted if the boundary adjoins a listed building or its curtilage, and demolition controls can matter in conservation areas.
rules.roof_rules: Across Somerset, boundary structures have no roof rule in the ordinary sense, yet anything fixed above the main enclosure line, such as trellis or pergola-style framing, can still affect the overall planning assessment.
rules.materials_rules: Across Somerset, no universal matching-material condition applies to fences and walls, but design still matters, especially on front boundaries. The more dominant the masonry, colour or finish, the more likely the structure is to draw planning attention.

restrictions.conservation_area: Boundary works in conservation areas are more sensitive because removal as well as replacement can affect the character and appearance of the area.
restrictions.listed_building: Listed building controls can apply to fences, gates and walls where they form part of the building's curtilage or historic setting.
restrictions.article4_notes: Article 4 directions and site-specific conditions are a common reason why an otherwise modest boundary change still needs planning permission.

rules.permitted_development: In Bath and North East Somerset, putting up or altering a fence, wall or gate is usually simplest where the overall height stays within the normal 2 metre limit, or 1 metre by a highway used by vehicles. Heritage controls and site-specific conditions can still take the proposal outside permitted development.

rules.height_rules: Height is the first check for fences and walls: 2 metres is the normal cap, reduced to 1 metre beside a highway used by vehicles or its footpath. Be careful with sloping ground or built-up levels, because the measurement is taken from ground level and not from the top of a bank.
rules.depth_rules: There is no separate depth allowance for fences and walls. What matters more is the line of the boundary, any change in ground level, and whether the structure starts to behave like retaining engineering rather than ordinary enclosure.
rules.boundary_rules: Boundary location matters as much as height. A wall or fence beside a vehicular access, on a corner plot or along a heritage frontage can still trigger separate planning concerns even when the basic limit is met.
rules.roof_rules: Boundary structures have no roof rule in the ordinary sense, yet anything fixed above the main enclosure line, such as trellis or pergola-style framing, can still affect the overall planning assessment.
rules.materials_rules: No universal matching-material condition applies to fences and walls, but design still matters, especially on front boundaries. The more dominant the masonry, colour or finish, the more likely the structure is to draw planning attention.

restrictions.conservation_area: In conservation areas, even modest boundary changes can need fuller scrutiny where an existing wall, railing or gate helps define the street scene.
restrictions.listed_building: Listed building controls can apply to fences, gates and walls where they form part of the building's curtilage or historic setting.
restrictions.article4_notes: A planning condition or Article 4 direction can override the standard boundary limits, so even a straightforward replacement fence may need consent.

rules.permitted_development: For homes in North Somerset, the standard fence and wall limits are 2 metres in most positions and 1 metre where the boundary is next to a highway used by vehicles. If the property is affected by listed-building controls, Article 4 restrictions or specific planning conditions, the ordinary householder route may not apply.

rules.height_rules: The main national height limits are 2 metres in most positions and 1 metre next to a highway used by vehicles. Height is measured from ground level, so raised beds, retaining walls or a sloping site can change the real planning answer.
rules.depth_rules: There is no separate depth allowance for fences and walls. What matters more is the line of the boundary, any change in ground level, and whether the structure starts to behave like retaining engineering rather than ordinary enclosure.
rules.boundary_rules: The enclosure may be permitted development on height, but still problematic on boundary position. Corner plots, access points, neighbouring listed curtilage and conservation-area demolition controls are all common complications.
rules.roof_rules: There is no separate roof allowance for a fence or wall. What often catches people out is that trellis, decorative tops, coping details and gate piers can still contribute to the measured height and prominence of the boundary.
rules.materials_rules: There is no blanket requirement to copy the house materials, although front boundaries generally work better when the walling, railings or panels feel in scale with the street rather than engineered or overbearing.

restrictions.conservation_area: A fence or wall in a conservation area may need more than a simple height check, especially if demolition of an older boundary is part of the scheme.
restrictions.listed_building: Historic boundary walls and railings are often part of a listed building's significance, so replacement or removal can need listed building consent.
restrictions.article4_notes: Normal enclosure rights can be withdrawn by Article 4 directions or by conditions on the property, which is why front-boundary work sometimes still needs an application.
